newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OLYMPICS-SOCOG SAYS BED TAX ROW HURTING BADLY.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-SOCOG SAYS BED TAX ROW HURTING BADLY.

text.p: Sydney 2000 Olympics organisers warned on Friday they could face serious cash flow and planning problems unless a row over a local hotel bed tax was quickly resolved.
The tax, which will add 10 percent to the cost of central Sydney hotel rooms from September, was passed by the New South Wales state parliament this week to fund Olympic construction.

But Sydney hoteliers, whose protests against the tax were ignored, are refusing to reach accomodation deals with organising committee SOCOG -- which needs to guarantee rooms to secure major international sponsors.
"It has reached a point now where it is seriously impeding our ability to sign up new sponsorships," SOCOG chief executive Sandy Hollway told a news conference.
"That means a problem potentially for flows of revenue and that in turn at some point has to impact on the amount we can spend.

"It is not at this stage a disaster -- we are not off the rails -- but I would be quite wrong to do other than point, quite publicly, to the fact that were the situation to become protracted, then we have a serious problem with managing the programme," Hollway said.

SOCOG president Michael Knight, who is also Olympics minister in the state government which introduced the tax, said SOCOG still had a projected A$600 million (US$450 million) to raise through sponsorship deals.
The NSW bed tax is designed to raise A$64 million a year.

About half of that money was being blocked by the "bed tax row", which forced SOCOG on Friday to suspend the signature of new sponsorship deals. One sponsor had already put a A$12 million cheque on hold, Knight said.

If the bed tax row does drag on and major sponsors are frightened off, the biggest loser would, ironically, be the local government and taxpayers. Under Sydney's Olympic contract, the state will underwrite any operating losses for the Games.
Knight and Hollway, who said the problem had to be solved within months, urged both the government and hotel industry to resolve the dispute as quickly as possible.
"We're the meat in the Olympic sandwich -- we just hope we won't be chomped on," Hollway said of the tussle.

Knight said he feared that Sydney hotels angered by the tax might now sign room deals with "ambush marketers" -- companies that were not official Olympic sponsors but could run marketing schemes on the back of the Games.
"Our biggest fear is that some elements in the hotel industry could go and sign up with ambush marketers," said Knight. "I appeal to the industry: don't go and sign up with the opposition."
The bed tax row is only the latest in a series of internal squabbles to hit the Sydney Olympic organisation, which has had almost a revolving door for senior executives.

In an attempt to prevent a repeat of last year's Atlanta fiasco -- when funding took priority over organisation -- the International Olympic Committee insisted that the NSW government be as involved as possible in the Sydney Games.
The IOC also pushed for the appointment of Knight, a politician, to head SOCOG even though Knight's party could well be voted out of office 18 months before the Games.
But since then, the Games' organisation has become increasingly politicised and the New South Wales opposition is now in open conflict with Knight over his handling of the Games. (AS1 = US$0.75)
